profile.reading:
CoreSite AT2 occupies 1130 Powers Ferry Place in Marietta, Georgia, north west of Atlanta inside Cobb County. CoreSite markets the building as AT2 Atlanta, but its own address line and its own specification sheet both place it in Marietta, and this entry uses the real location rather than the metro label. Jurisdiction is worth pinning down as well. The adjoining parcel at 1155 Powers Ferry Place was rezoned by the Marietta City Council rather than the Cobb County Board of Commissioners, which places this block inside city limits, although the registry row still records the county.

The building dates to 2018 according to local reporting, and it has changed hands twice since. It opened as DataSite Atlanta. American Tower acquired DataSite from Burges Property Company in October 2021 for 201 million dollars, taking two buildings, this one and a 130,000 square foot facility on South John Young Parkway in Orlando. In June 2022 American Tower transferred three of its own data centres into CoreSite, the downtown Atlanta carrier hotel at 55 Marietta Street known as AT1, this Marietta building as AT2, and the Orlando site as OR1, more than 250,000 square feet between them. CoreSite itself became an American Tower subsidiary at the end of 2021, and Stonepeak later took a minority position in American Tower's United States data centre business.

On the four power numbers this entry has to say something unsatisfying and say it plainly. CoreSite publishes no megawatt figure for AT2 at all. Its facility page and its own specification sheet give 67,000 plus square feet, cabinets, cages and private suites with no partial cabinet product, alternating current power, diverse underground utility feeds from the grid, N plus 1 redundancy on UPS, power distribution units and remote power panels, N plus 1 and 2N on generators, N plus 1 on chillers, pumps and computer room air handlers, variable speed air handlers with humidification control, and Trane and York air cooled chillers. It lists SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS and HIPAA, and access to AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect and Oracle FastConnect through its Open Cloud Exchange. It describes AT2 as a stand alone facility rather than part of a campus. Nowhere does it state an IT load, a utility service rating, a UPS rating or a generator rating. The only megawatt number in circulation is a 4.6 megawatt figure published by trade analysis at the time of the DataSite acquisition alongside a 73,000 square foot area, and that figure appears with no statement of what it measures, so it is recorded here as unlabelled and is not stored as capacity of any kind.

The local record around the building has become unusually active. On 9 July 2026 the Marietta City Council tabled a rezoning for 1155 Powers Ferry Place, where Prime Storage, a subsidiary of Prime Group Holdings of Saratoga Springs, New York, proposed converting part of a roughly 90,000 square foot self storage building on about 11 acres into a data centre, and the same night imposed a unanimous six month citywide moratorium on new data centre applications running through 31 December 2026, exempting anything already filed or approved. On 13 August 2026 the council approved that rezoning anyway by five votes to two, precisely because the application predated the freeze. The project is described as 18 megawatts. The city's own analysis conceded that Marietta's zoning code contains no standards specific to data centres and that the applicant's noise enclosure commitment carried no specifics, and residents raised the effect on Rottenwood Creek. Unincorporated Cobb County has moved separately, extending its own moratorium to 24 February 2027, with the agenda item noting that the county's 1972 code gives no consideration to this land use and currently treats data centres like warehouses or private utilities in light and heavy industrial districts, and that no data centre had yet been formally proposed in unincorporated Cobb.

State level context matters here too. The Georgia Public Service Commission froze Georgia Power base rates from 31 July 2025 through 2028, stating that the purpose is to prevent new data centres from shifting costs to residential customers, and a January 2025 large load rule allows minimum billing requirements and longer contract terms and requires Georgia Power to file every data centre contract with the commission at least thirty days before signing. Approved generation need in Georgia moved from a 2022 estimate of 400 megawatts over seven years to 9,985 megawatts approved in December 2025, roughly 80 percent of it attributed to data centres. AT2 belongs to none of that. It is a small interconnection building that predates the wave and would be an unremarkable tenant of it.

One further unknown is worth stating rather than glossing. Marietta runs its own municipal electric utility, Marietta Power, established by the city in 1906 and serving more than 45,000 customers in Marietta and Cobb County under the Marietta Board of Lights and Water. A building inside city limits is therefore not automatically a Georgia Power customer, and neither CoreSite nor the city publishes which utility serves 1130 Powers Ferry Place. The year the building was fitted out, its tenant list and every one of its four power numbers likewise remain unpublished.

profile.regulatory_note: Address is 1130 Powers Ferry Place, Marietta, Georgia, in Cobb County. The adjoining parcel at 1155 Powers Ferry Place was rezoned by the Marietta City Council rather than the Cobb County Board of Commissioners, indicating this block sits inside Marietta city limits. Marietta's zoning code contains no standards specific to data centres, a point the city's own staff analysis acknowledged in August 2026. reading.body:
CoreSite AT2 publishes 67,000 square feet of technical space but no power figure, making it impossible to assess its contribution to AI infrastructure without assumptions the operator has not supplied.

The 67,000-square-foot footprint places AT2 in the mid-sized colocation range, suitable for enterprise workloads but not in the hyperscale category now driving AI compute deployment. Without a megawatt figure, the square footage alone cannot translate to racks, GPU density, or AI training capacity. That gap matters because power density varies by workload and cooling design, and the operator chose not to publish either.

The facility holds six compliance certifications spanning financial services, payment processing, health data, information security, and federal security standards. These qualifications serve regulated enterprises and their data but do not signal readiness for large-scale AI training. AI infrastructure specifications like power redundancy tier, cooling architecture, and GPU-to-rack configuration are absent from the published profile.

Georgia's index shows 33 facilities statewide, but only 2 publish megawatt figures, totaling 42 MW combined. AT2's missing power data means Georgia appears as a thin compute picture for AI, and whether AT2 adds materially to that figure remains unknown. For readers tracking grid constraints on AI scaling, a state where the largest facilities hide their power consumption is a state that has not yet made its capacity visible to the market.
